drivetrain.caveat: Free speed is the unloaded ceiling and stall thrust ignores traction limits; both need a real current-limited simulation before you trust them.
drivetrain.encoder: CANcoder, SRX Mag, Thrifty AME or Helium Canandmag on the azimuth
drivetrain.selection_reason: SDS MK5i chosen as the default for a 4 in wheel

intake.deploy: powered pivot with metal hard stops

hopper.floor: 0.093 in polycarbonate floor plate over a plate frame
hopper.sensor: beam-break at the exit gate, one staged piece at a time
hopper.access: thumbscrew top panel so a jam clears without removing the shooter
hopper.caveat: Capacity is volumetric: floor area × 80% of the wall height × 60% random-pour packing, divided by one gamepiece. The real limit is usually what the exit lane clears without jamming, not what the box holds. Feed rate is a geometric ceiling — measure it with a full hopper while driving the obstacles.

shooter.wheel: grey 60A urethane flywheels on a 1/2 in hex shaft

shot.caveat: Vacuum trajectory: no drag, no spin, no Magnus. A foam ball loses real range to air, so treat this as the optimistic ceiling and tune on the field.

shooter.feed_path: hopper → feeder tower → feeder → flywheel pair → hood

elevator.bearing_blocks: opposed, preloaded at every stage interface
elevator.carriage: bolted carriage on the final stage
elevator.load_path: carriage → final stage → rigging → drum → gearbox

manipulator.gravity_compensation: feedforward sized on the horizontal holding case
manipulator.pivot: dead axle with serviceable bearing blocks

rise.mode: hoist the robot, not reach the rung

criteria.L1: no longer touching the carpet or the TOWER BASE
criteria.L2: BUMPER covers completely above the LOW RUNG (27 in)
criteria.L3: BUMPER covers completely above the MID RUNG (45 in)

rise.note: Levels score on where the robot's bumper covers end up, not on what it touches, and the height cap forbids extending to the rung. The mechanism grips a rung and lifts the whole robot; re-gripping one rung higher (18 in) is what earns the next level.

climber.tower: 2x2x0.125 in upright tied into two rails
climber.rope: 1/8 in Dyneema on a grooved drum
climber.engagement: easy in, hard out: free entry, bears under load
climber.bearing_blocks: rolling blocks at both ends of every stage overlap
climber.ratchet: mechanical ratchet on the winch drum

constraints.rule_snapshot: Limits shown are the published 2026 REBUILT figures. Rules move by team update — verify perimeter, height, extension, motor count and weight against the current manual before inspection.

season.label: 2026 REBUILT

gamepiece.name: fuel
gamepiece.handling: A 5.91 in sphere rolls, nests and is handled in bulk — the design problem is throughput and jam-free indexing, not single-piece precision. Foam wears: a ball late in an event compresses more easily than a fresh one, so a shooter tuned on day one drifts.

season.summary: Two alliances score FUEL into their HUB, cross a BUMP or a TRENCH between zones, and climb the TOWER at the end of the match. A HUB only pays while it is active, so cycle timing and passing matter as much as raw capacity.

match.note: HUBs alternate between active and inactive; all HUBs go active as time runs out. Scoring capacity is worth nothing during an inactive window, which is what makes passing and stealing real strategies.

ranking.name: ENERGIZED
ranking.threshold: FUEL in the active HUB: 100 regional / 240 DCMP / 360 CMP

ranking.name: SUPERCHARGED
ranking.threshold: FUEL in the active HUB: 360 regional / 360 DCMP / 500 CMP

ranking.name: TRAVERSAL
ranking.threshold: 50 TOWER points in the match (all levels)

field_elements.name: HUB
field_elements.note: A 47 × 47 in prism with a 41.7 in hexagonal opening whose front edge is 72 in off the carpet. The shot has to arrive above that edge and still be descending into the opening. The design and long ranges are Kale's sizing assumptions, not field dimensions: 18 ft is a comfortable working distance and 30 ft is roughly a cross-zone shot. Set them from where your strategy actually shoots.

field_elements.name: TOWER

level_criteria.L1: no longer touching the carpet or the TOWER BASE
level_criteria.L2: BUMPER covers completely above the LOW RUNG (27 in)
level_criteria.L3: BUMPER covers completely above the MID RUNG (45 in)

field_elements.note: Two uprights 32.25 in apart carry three 1.66 in OD pipe rungs at 27, 45 and 63 in, 18 in apart, each overhanging 5.875 in past the upright face. Levels are scored on where the ROBOT's BUMPERS are, not on what it touches: L2 needs the bumpers entirely above the 27 in rung and L3 entirely above the 45 in rung, while contacting a rung or upright. The robot hoists its own body up the tower — it does not extend a mast, because R107 caps total height at 30 in the whole time. Supporting structure crosses from upright to wall between 28.40 and 43.38 in, which a climbing robot has to clear.

field_elements.name: DEPOT
field_elements.note: 42 × 27 in bounded by 3 in steel barriers — an intake wider than the opening cannot sweep it cleanly.

field_elements.name: BUMP
field_elements.note: A 6.513 in crest on 15° ramps. Ground clearance and wheelbase decide whether a robot drives over it or beaches on it, and a full hopper spills across the crest.

field_elements.name: TRENCH
field_elements.note: The underpass is 50.34 in wide and 22.25 in tall. A robot that fits under it has a second route between zones; one that does not is committed to the BUMP.

design_targets.means: A square frame is at most 27.5 in on a side. Pick the rectangle deliberately — a wider frame buys intake width, a longer one buys mechanism room, and the budget spends on one or the other.
Everything, climber included, has to stow inside this before the match starts.

This is not a starting-configuration limit — nothing may extend above it at any point in the match. It rules out a tall elevator and a telescoping climb mast outright. Measured perpendicular to the robot perimeter as if the robot were on a flat floor, which is why hanging partway up the TOWER is still legal: the robot's own height has not changed.
Sets how far an intake or a turret may reach outside the frame. A turret whose shooter sweeps past the perimeter is the classic way to fail this.
Budget it per subsystem at design time; a weight problem found in week six is a redesign.
Motors that drive the robot across the carpet. Swerve steering motors do not count, so four modules are fine — but a six-motor west-coast drivebase is not.

design_targets.from: HUB opening front edge at 72 in
design_targets.means: From a release around 21 in the ball has to gain 51 in and still be falling when it arrives. A flat shot at rim height hits the edge; aim for an entry angle past 40°.
A 41.7 in target is forgiving in azimuth and unforgiving in range — distance error, not heading error, is what misses.

design_targets.value: L2 ≥ 39 in of rise, L3 ≥ 57 in
design_targets.from: TOWER scoring criteria + R405 bumper zone
design_targets.means: Levels are scored on the ROBOT's position, not its reach: L2 needs the bumper covers entirely above the 45 in rung and L3 entirely above the 63 in rung, while contacting a rung or upright. With the bumper top at 5.75 in on the ground, that is the whole robot rising 57+ in for L3. Rungs are 18 in apart, so a mechanism that can re-grip one rung higher earns one more level.
1-1/4 in Sch 40 pipe, overhanging 5.875 in past each upright face. Size the hook throat to that OD, and expect the support structure crossing between 28.4 and 43.38 in to be in the way on the way up.

A robot under 22.25 in gets a second route between zones. That is a whole-robot decision made at architecture time, not a trim you apply later — the hopper, the shooter and the climber all have to live in it.
Breakover, not ground clearance, is what beaches a robot: a long wheelbase lands its belly on the crest. Check the diagonal, and expect a loaded hopper to spill going over.

scoring_math: An L3 climb is 30 points — the same as 30 FUEL, which at a realistic 4–6 FUEL per second of *active* HUB time is roughly six seconds of perfect scoring. A climb that takes longer than that and costs you the last active window is not free.
An auto L1 climb is 15 points for two robots, so an alliance that climbs in auto banks 30 points before teleop and only needs 20 more TOWER points for TRAVERSAL.
TRAVERSAL needs 50 TOWER points: L2 + L3 (50) does it, as does auto L1 ×2 (30) plus any single teleop climb.
ENERGIZED at 100 FUEL is an alliance total — roughly 33 per robot, which a competent cycler clears. SUPERCHARGED at 360 is 3.6× that and is an alliance strategy, not a robot specification.
FUEL in an inactive HUB is worth zero. Capacity you cannot deliver during an active window is dead weight, which is the argument for passing and for storing.

archetypes.name: Turreted cycler
archetypes.shape: over-bumper intake → spindexer → feeder tower → turret + hooded shooter → L2/L3 climb
archetypes.why: A turret decouples aiming from driving, so the robot can shoot while crossing and can pass to a partner without turning. It costs a slew bearing, a wire-management path and a zeroing procedure.
archetypes.against: Complexity and packaging; a turret that leaves the frame perimeter is illegal.

archetypes.name: Fixed wide shooter
archetypes.shape: wide intake → twin-lane hopper → two fixed hooded shooters → climb
archetypes.why: Two lanes double throughput without a turret, and a fixed shooter is far simpler to build, wire and tune.
archetypes.against: The drivebase has to aim, so every shot costs a rotation and defence hurts more.

archetypes.name: Low-profile trench runner
archetypes.shape: under-22.25 in envelope, flat hopper, low shooter, L1/L2 climb
archetypes.why: Fitting under the TRENCH gives a route the tall robots cannot take, which is worth more than a few points of capacity in a congested match.
archetypes.against: Everything has to live under 22.25 in, which fights hopper volume and shot angle.

archetypes.name: Defender / feeder
archetypes.shape: fast drivebase, wide floor intake, shuttling shooter, quick L1 climb
archetypes.why: Denying an active HUB window is worth as much as scoring in it, and shuttling fuel to a partner converts your floor time into their points.
archetypes.against: Scores little on its own; needs a strong alliance and a good driver.

season.verify: Figures are the published field and rule values for 2026 REBUILT. Rules move by team update during the season — check the current manual and every team update before you cut metal or go to inspection.

reference_basis.name: 2025 Serpentheim CAD Release
reference_basis.lesson: 2x1 tube chassis; subsystem hierarchy; rigid assemblies and explicit mates

reference_basis.name: 6328 Crescendo shooter / robot
reference_basis.lesson: split flywheel sides, feeder path, serviceable side plates

reference_basis.name: 2910 Rapid React robot
reference_basis.lesson: hood, feeder and climber as separate top-level assemblies

reference_basis.name: FRCDesign coaxial slapdown intake
reference_basis.lesson: static gearbox, rigid arm, top-level revolute mate and powered roller path

reference_basis.name: FRCDesign roller-intake reference
reference_basis.lesson: roller center distance sets compression; series rollers hand off to an indexer; surface speed geared above approach speed; compliant-wheel durometer matched to the gamepiece; metal hard stops on the deploy arc

reference_basis.name: 2025 REV ION Starter Bot
reference_basis.lesson: manufacturable single-stage elevator, wrist and intake packaging

reference_basis.name: FRCDesign mechanism library
reference_basis.lesson: layout sketches, dead axles, power transmission and subsystem boundaries

reference_basis.name: WCP / REV structural tube and gusset catalog
reference_basis.lesson: model to stock sections — 2x1x0.100, 1x1, 2x2x0.125 — so a cut list is orderable; gussets in double shear at every bolted corner

reference_basis.name: 2026 FRC Game Manual
reference_basis.lesson: current starting perimeter, height, bumper, safety and extension constraints

reference_basis.name: WCP GreyT turret
reference_basis.lesson: a turret is one large-bore bearing plus plate bearing blocks and a driven ring; the hard part is the wire path under the plate, not the rotation

reference_basis.name: Open-alliance spindexer and hopper build threads
reference_basis.lesson: bulk ball indexing converges on a rotating floor that feeds one lane: raise the driven wheels slightly above the floor, funnel many lanes into one, and gate the last piece with a sensor rather than a timer

reference_basis.name: Public team CAD and technical binder releases
reference_basis.lesson: a technical binder states, per subsystem: the requirement, the options considered, the calculation that chose between them, the test that validated it and the failure mode still open — write the design that way and the review takes minutes

techniques.name: Belly pan as a shear panel
techniques.why: A four-rail rectangle racks under impact; a bolted plate makes it rigid.
techniques.how: Pocket a 0.090 in plate and bolt it to every rail, not just the corners.
techniques.pitfall: Pocketing away the bolt-line material and losing the shear path.

techniques.name: Bolt-together over welded frames
techniques.why: A welded frame that bends is scrap; a bolted one is a replaced rail.
techniques.how: Gussets in double shear at every corner, rivets or 10-32 through both walls.
techniques.pitfall: Loading rivets in tension instead of shear.

techniques.name: Reserve the module corners first
techniques.why: Swerve corners are non-negotiable volume; everything else moves around them.
techniques.how: Place the four module envelopes before any mechanism sketch exists.
techniques.pitfall: Routing a mechanism through a corner and discovering it at assembly.

techniques.name: Current limits before gear ratios
techniques.why: The battery, not the motor curve, sets what the drivetrain can actually do.
techniques.how: Set a per-motor supply limit, then pick the ratio that hits your target speed.
techniques.pitfall: Choosing a fast ratio, browning out, and blaming the code.

techniques.name: Dedicated drivetrain CAN bus
techniques.why: Eight modules of status frames will saturate a shared bus.
techniques.how: Put drive and steer controllers on a CANivore, leave mechanisms on the RIO bus.
techniques.pitfall: Debugging 'random' drivetrain stutter that is really bus utilisation.

techniques.name: Azimuth zeroing procedure
techniques.why: A module that boots at the wrong angle drives into the wall on enable.
techniques.how: Absolute encoder offsets stored in code, with a documented physical zeroing jig.
techniques.pitfall: Re-zeroing by feel after every belt change.

techniques.name: One main breaker, no bypasses
techniques.why: It is the only guaranteed way to kill the robot, and it is inspected.
techniques.how: Battery + goes to the main breaker, breaker to the distributor, nothing else.
techniques.pitfall: Tapping power upstream of the breaker for 'just one' accessory.

techniques.name: Wire gauge follows the breaker, not the motor
techniques.why: The breaker decides how much current the wire will ever be asked to carry.
techniques.how: 40 A channel → 10 AWG, 30 A → 12 AWG, 10 A accessories → 18 AWG.
techniques.pitfall: 18 AWG on a 40 A channel because it was the spool on the table.

techniques.name: Service loops and strain relief
techniques.why: Wires break at the crimp when a mechanism pulls on them.
techniques.how: Leave slack at every moving joint and anchor the harness on both sides of it.
techniques.pitfall: A taut wire across a pivot that survives testing and fails in a match.

techniques.name: Radio placement is an RF decision
techniques.why: Aluminium shadows and motor noise cause 'random' disconnects.
techniques.how: Mount high, antennas clear on both faces, away from motors and CAN bundles.
techniques.pitfall: Bolting it flat to the bellypan under the battery.

techniques.name: Layout sketch first
techniques.why: Every downstream part references it, so changes stay cheap.
techniques.how: One master sketch per subsystem carrying the critical dimensions.
techniques.pitfall: Modelling parts directly and re-cutting them for every revision.

techniques.name: Subassembly = one rigid body
techniques.why: It makes mates solve and mirrors how the robot is actually assembled.
techniques.how: Rigid-group everything that does not move relative to its neighbours.
techniques.pitfall: Top-level assemblies with hundreds of loose parts.

techniques.name: Mate the way it bolts together
techniques.why: The assembly order in CAD should be the order on the build table.
techniques.how: Fastened mates for bolted joints, revolute for pivots, slider for stages.
techniques.pitfall: Position-only mates that hide an interference.

techniques.name: Model to stock, not to shape
techniques.why: A part that is not a stock section or a plate outline cannot be made in a school shop, and you find that out at fabrication instead of at review.
techniques.how: Every structural member is a catalog section — 2x1x0.100, 1x1, 2x2x0.125 — cut to a length you can write on a cut list. Everything else is 2D plate.
techniques.pitfall: A 1.375 in square tube that exists in no supplier's catalog.

techniques.name: One datum per mechanism
techniques.why: Bearings that are located off three different faces never line up, and the shaft binds no matter how carefully each part was made.
techniques.how: Pick one plate per mechanism as the datum and locate every bore from it; the opposite plate is a mirrored copy, not an independently dimensioned part.
techniques.pitfall: Dimensioning the second side plate from the first side plate's edge.

techniques.name: Centre distances are the design, holes are the consequence
techniques.why: Belt and gear centre distances are set by the reduction and the pitch; if you place the holes first you get a ratio nobody can buy a belt for.
techniques.how: Solve the centre distance from tooth counts and pitch, then place the bores. For HTD 5 mm, pitch diameter is teeth × 5 / π mm.
techniques.pitfall: Rounding a centre distance to a nice number and tensioning the belt to death.

techniques.name: Fastener access is geometry
techniques.why: A bolt you cannot get a wrench on is a bolt that never gets torqued, and the joint it holds is the one that fails at the first hard hit.
techniques.how: Check a 1/4 in hex driver's swept cylinder at every fastener before the design is closed; move the hole, not the tool.
techniques.pitfall: Discovering at assembly that the gearbox has to come off to reach a rail bolt.

techniques.name: Compression is the design variable
techniques.why: Too little and it never grabs; too much and it stalls or damages the gamepiece.
techniques.how: Start near 0.5 in of compression on compliant wheels and tune on a test rig.
techniques.pitfall: Setting compression by eye at 2 am and never measuring it.

techniques.name: Coaxial pivot power
techniques.why: Running roller power through the pivot axis removes a whole tensioning problem.
techniques.how: Belt to a shaft on the pivot centreline, then out to the roller.
techniques.pitfall: Non-coaxial routing whose belt tension changes through the deploy arc.

techniques.name: Hard stops in metal, not in software
techniques.why: Software limits fail when the encoder does.
techniques.how: A physical stop at each end of the deploy arc plus a current-limited hold.
techniques.pitfall: A 40 A motor grinding against a plastic stop.

techniques.name: Surface speed must beat approach speed
techniques.why: A roller slower than the robot's floor speed shoves the gamepiece away instead of pulling it in.
techniques.how: Gear the roller so its surface speed (roller RPM x pi x diameter) is 1.5-2x the fastest intended approach speed; a 2 in roller off a NEO through ~4:1 clears this easily.
techniques.pitfall: A direct-driven roller that stalls the motor and still cannot out-run the drivebase.

techniques.name: Center distance sets compression, not eyeballing
techniques.why: Compression is a dimension you cut into the plates, not a feel you dial in at 2 am.
techniques.how: Fix the roller-to-bumper (or roller-to-roller) center distance so free wheel radius minus gap equals ~0.5 in of squish on a compliant wheel; put it in the layout sketch.
techniques.pitfall: Slotted mounts 'adjusted to feel', so every rebuild grabs differently.

techniques.name: Durometer picks the wheel, not diameter alone
techniques.why: A soft compliant wheel conforms and grips; a hard one skips over a rigid gamepiece.
techniques.how: Softer (30-35A green compliant) for hard/heavy pieces, firmer (40A+) for light foam; match the wheel to the gamepiece and keep spares — they wear.
techniques.pitfall: One durometer chosen for spin-up that never actually grabs the game piece.

techniques.name: Two-roller handoff into an indexer
techniques.why: A single roller acquires; a second staged roller controls the piece into the feeder.
techniques.how: Series rollers geared to increasing surface speed, then a positive indexer stage with a beam-break so the shooter/elevator gets one piece at a known position.
techniques.pitfall: One fast roller that flings acquired pieces straight back out or jams two at once.

techniques.name: Over-bumper vs under-bumper is a geometry decision
techniques.why: The two solve different floor-clearance and deploy-volume problems, not style.
techniques.how: Over-bumper reaches down past the bumper on a pivot for tall/rolling pieces; under-bumper stays low and fixed for flat pieces but needs a bumper gap cut.
techniques.pitfall: Copying a top team's over-bumper arm for a gamepiece that a fixed roller would grab.

techniques.name: One lane out, however many lanes in
techniques.why: A shooter can only take one gamepiece at a time. Every mechanism that tries to hand it two at once jams, and the jam always happens under load in a match.
techniques.how: Funnel the floor into a single exit lane, and make the last stage before the shooter positive — a driven roller or belt that owns the piece — with a beam-break telling the code exactly one is staged.
techniques.pitfall: A wide hopper that dumps straight into the feeder and wedges two pieces in the throat.

techniques.name: Raise the driven wheels above the floor
techniques.why: A rotating-floor indexer works by driving the gamepiece across a stationary surface. If the wheels are flush the piece rides on the floor and slips; too high and it climbs over.
techniques.how: Set the wheel axis so roughly half an inch of wheel stands above the floor plate for a 6 in ball, then test with a full hopper, not one piece.
techniques.pitfall: Tuning the indexer with three gamepieces and finding it stalls with twelve.

techniques.name: Test the hopper full, and test it on the bump
techniques.why: Throughput measured with a half-empty hopper is fiction: the pieces at the bottom carry the weight of the ones above them, and driving over an obstacle throws the whole mass at one wall.
techniques.how: Fill it to capacity, drive the real field obstacles, and count pieces per second out of the exit rather than watching it spin.
techniques.pitfall: A hopper that indexes beautifully on the bench and packs solid in a match.

techniques.name: Compression is the jam knob
techniques.why: Indexer compression trades throughput against current draw and jamming. Too loose and pieces slip; too tight and the motor heats, the bus sags and the pieces wedge.
techniques.how: Set it as a dimension in the plates, then back it off in small steps while watching supply current until throughput stops improving.
techniques.pitfall: Chasing jams by tightening compression, which is usually what caused them.

techniques.name: Give the hopper a floor you can open
techniques.why: Every bulk handler jams eventually, and a jam you can clear in ten seconds between matches is a different problem from one that needs the shooter removed.
techniques.how: Make one wall or the top plate a thumbscrew panel, and keep the exit lane visible.
techniques.pitfall: A sealed hopper that has to come off the robot to clear one wedged piece.

techniques.name: Recovery time over top speed
techniques.why: Cycle rate is set by how fast the wheel returns to setpoint after a shot.
techniques.how: Add flywheel inertia and headroom rather than chasing peak RPM.
techniques.pitfall: A fast, light wheel that needs two seconds between shots.

techniques.name: Split-side flywheels
techniques.why: Independent sides let you spin the gamepiece and correct drift.
techniques.how: Separate motors per side, coupled only through the gamepiece.
techniques.pitfall: One shaft across both sides that makes spin impossible.

techniques.name: Serviceable side plates
techniques.why: You will pull the flywheel more than once during competition.
techniques.how: Bolt-on plates, dowel-located, that come off without dropping the shaft.
techniques.pitfall: A shooter you have to disassemble the robot to reach.

techniques.name: Exit velocity is half the surface speed, with one wheel
techniques.why: A gamepiece squeezed between a spinning wheel and a stationary hood leaves at roughly the mean of the two surfaces, so a single wheel gives half its own surface speed — teams routinely size a shooter as if it gave all of it.
techniques.how: Compute surface speed as free RPM ÷ reduction × π × wheel diameter, then halve it for a hooded single wheel, or keep it for counter-rotating pairs.
techniques.pitfall: A shooter geared for a range it can only reach on paper.

techniques.name: Compression sets the energy transfer
techniques.why: Too little compression and the wheel slips on the gamepiece; too much and the wheel stalls and the shot is short and inconsistent.
techniques.how: Set the wheel-to-hood gap about half an inch under the gamepiece diameter and make the hood adjustable so it can be tuned on the practice field.
techniques.pitfall: A welded-position hood that cannot be tuned once the game piece wears in.

techniques.name: Stage a barrel shooter so each pair adds speed
techniques.why: A staged barrel accelerates progressively instead of dumping all the energy in one impulse, which is gentler on the gamepiece and easier on the motors.
techniques.how: Each successive flywheel pair runs faster than the one before it and the pairs sit one gamepiece diameter apart down the barrel.
techniques.pitfall: Running every stage at the same speed, so the later pairs just drag.

techniques.name: Turret on one large-bore bearing
techniques.why: A turret carries moment loads, not just rotation; a stack of small bearings wobbles.
techniques.how: One large-diameter X-contact or lazy-susan style bearing under the whole turret, driven by a geared ring or a capstan drive for low backlash.
techniques.pitfall: A cantilevered turret on a single small bearing that shakes the shot loose.

techniques.name: Turret wire management with hard stops
techniques.why: A turret that spins freely rips its own harness out mid-match.
techniques.how: Limit rotation with physical hard stops and a wire-wrap service loop sized for the full sweep, or fit a slip ring if continuous rotation is genuinely needed.
techniques.pitfall: Software-only rotation limits guarding a taut cable bundle.

techniques.name: Stage the acceleration down a barrel
techniques.why: One impulse from a single flywheel pair wastes energy in slip and scuffs the gamepiece; several pairs in series each add a little speed.
techniques.how: Run 2-3 flywheel pairs down a guided barrel at increasing surface speed, each pair lightly compressed, so the piece leaves at the sum of the stages.
techniques.pitfall: Stages geared the same speed, so later pairs brake the piece instead of driving it.

techniques.name: Guide the piece, don't just launch it
techniques.why: Exit angle repeatability comes from the guide path, not from the wheels.
techniques.how: Constrain the piece through the whole barrel with polycarbonate guides and a fixed exit lip; keep the last stage closest to the exit.
techniques.pitfall: An open path where the piece rattles and every shot leaves at a different angle.

techniques.name: Zero the turret like a swerve azimuth
techniques.why: A turret that boots at the wrong angle aims at your own alliance wall.
techniques.how: Absolute encoder on the azimuth with stored offsets and a documented zeroing jig.
techniques.pitfall: Re-zeroing by eye in the pit and trusting it in the match.

techniques.name: Ratchet or brake before you need it
techniques.why: A winch that back-drives drops the robot.
techniques.how: Mechanical ratchet on the drum, not just motor brake mode.
techniques.pitfall: Relying on brake mode after the match ends and power cuts.

techniques.name: Load path into the frame
techniques.why: The climber carries the entire robot weight through whatever it is bolted to.
techniques.how: Tie the tower into two rails and the bellypan, in shear.
techniques.pitfall: A tower bolted to a single crossmember that folds.

techniques.name: Size the winch on drum torque, not motor torque
techniques.why: The drum radius is a lever working against you: rope tension times drum radius is the torque the gearbox has to hold, and a bigger drum makes it worse.
techniques.how: Tension is robot weight ÷ load paths; drum torque is tension × drum radius; the reduction is that torque divided by what the motors give at a safe duty point, not at stall.
techniques.pitfall: A 2 in drum chosen for rope capacity that doubles the required reduction.

techniques.name: Two load paths beat one strong one
techniques.why: Two hooks halve the tension in each rope and stop the robot swinging on a single point, which is what usually pulls a hook out of the cage.
techniques.how: Dual telescoping hooks on a common shaft so they pay out together.
techniques.pitfall: Two independent winches that drift out of sync and cock the robot.

techniques.name: Stow inside the starting volume
techniques.why: It is an inspection failure, not a design preference.
techniques.how: Check the stowed height against the current manual before committing.
techniques.pitfall: Discovering it at inspection on Thursday.

techniques.name: Easy in, hard out cage engagement
techniques.why: A deep-cage or bar hook must enter with almost no resistance and resist exit under load.
techniques.how: Barb or hook geometry that slips in freely, then bears on a groove or shoulder when the winch loads it, pull-test the engagement before trusting it at the buzzer.
techniques.pitfall: A hook that binds on entry in the last ten seconds, or slips out under swing.

techniques.name: Bearing blocks between telescoping stages
techniques.why: Metal-on-metal telescopes seize the moment a side load appears mid-climb.
techniques.how: Rolling bearings or Delrin blocks at both ends of every stage overlap, taking load in both directions.
techniques.pitfall: A telescope that extends freely on the bench and jams under the robot's weight.

techniques.name: One-way bearing power take-off
techniques.why: Sharing one motor between a shooter and a winch saves a motor, a breaker and a channel.
techniques.how: Winch pulley on a one-way bearing on the shooter shaft: forward free-wheels for shooting, reverse locks the bearing and drives the winch.
techniques.pitfall: An unguarded PTO that engages the winch every time the shooter reverses to clear a jam.

techniques.name: One large-bore bearing carries the whole turret
techniques.why: A turret carries moment loads, not just rotation; a stack of small bearings wobbles and the shot walks.
techniques.how: One large-diameter slew or X-contact bearing under the turret plate, driven by a ring gear or a capstan for low backlash.
techniques.pitfall: A cantilevered turret on one small bearing that shakes the aim loose over a match.

techniques.name: The wire path is the design problem
techniques.why: The bearing is the easy part. Getting motor power, CAN and a camera across a rotating joint without tearing a harness is what actually takes the time.
techniques.how: An energy chain or a service loop sized for the full sweep, tensioned by a constant-force spring so it never goes slack and snags, with physical rotation limits at both ends. A slip ring only if continuous rotation is genuinely needed.
techniques.pitfall: Software-only rotation limits guarding a taut cable bundle.

techniques.name: Keep the sweep inside the frame perimeter
techniques.why: A turret that swings a shooter past the perimeter is an extension-rule failure at inspection, not a packaging annoyance.
techniques.how: Sweep the widest point of the turret through its full range in CAD against the perimeter and the extension allowance before committing the plate size.
techniques.pitfall: Discovering at inspection that the hood clears the bumper at 45°.

techniques.name: Zero the azimuth like a swerve module
techniques.why: A turret that boots at the wrong angle aims at your own alliance wall.
techniques.how: Absolute encoder on the azimuth with stored offsets and a documented zeroing jig.
techniques.pitfall: Re-zeroing by eye in the pit and trusting it in the match.

techniques.name: Decide what the turret is for before building one
techniques.why: A turret buys shoot-while-moving and passing without turning. If the strategy does not use either, it is mass, complexity and a wire path for nothing.
techniques.how: Write down the two or three match situations that justify it. If a fixed shooter and a good driver cover them, build the fixed shooter.
techniques.pitfall: Building a turret because the top teams have one, then aiming with the drivebase anyway.

intent: 27x27 swerve on Kraken X60s, turreted variable-hood flywheel shooter for 25 ft shots, serpentine tunnel indexer, L3 tower climb.

notes: Summed stall current across every motor is 5232 A. That is an arithmetic worst case, not a real operating point, no battery sources it and the robot never stalls everything at once.

The number to design against: on a nominal 12 mΩ battery the bus reaches the ~6.8 V brownout threshold at roughly 433 A total draw. Set per-motor current limits so realistic simultaneous draw stays well under that.
The 120 A main breaker trips long before the summed stall figure, and every branch runs through it, nothing bypasses it except the battery lead itself.
Battery internal resistance rises sharply as a battery ages; an old battery browns out at a current a fresh one handles.

mass_estimate.caveat: First-order estimate from envelope masses and typical subsystem weights, compared against the target without bumpers or battery. It is for early trade studies only, weigh the real robot, and check what your season's manual actually excludes.

rule_check.detail: 27 × 27 in = 108 in against a 110 in budget
rule_check.fix: Shrink to 27.5 in square or any rectangle summing to 55 in per side pair.

rule_check.detail: tallest stowed feature 29 in against 30 in
rule_check.fix: Fold, telescope or lower the tall subsystem into the starting envelope; this is an inspection failure, not a preference.

rule_check.detail: tallest deployed feature 30 in against a 30 in limit that applies for the whole match
rule_check.fix: Nothing may extend above this at any time — not a mast, not an elevator, not a climb hook. A climber has to raise the robot's own body up the structure instead of reaching up to it.

rule_check.detail: 4 propulsion motors against a limit of 4 (swerve steering motors do not count)
rule_check.fix: Drop to 4 driven motors — for a west-coast drivebase that means 4 motors across both gearboxes, not six.
Estimates are for trade studies. Weigh the real robot before you rely on this.
